clinicalPearls: Defined as the sudden and unexpected death of an infant under one year that remains unexplained after a thorough death scene investigation, review of history, and complete postmortem examination.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion and forms part of the broader category of sudden unexpected infant death (SUID).
Incidence peaks between about 2 and 4 months of age, and most deaths occur during sleep.
Prone and side sleeping positions are major modifiable risk factors; supine sleep is strongly protective.
Additional risks include soft bedding, bed-sharing, overheating, maternal smoking during and after pregnancy, prematurity, and low birth weight.
Protective measures include breastfeeding, immunisation, pacifier use at sleep, and room-sharing without bed-sharing.
The prevailing model proposes a vulnerable infant meeting an exogenous stressor during a critical developmental period (the triple-risk hypothesis).
Safe-sleep counselling for every family is a core preventive intervention, and any death requires a compassionate, thorough investigation to exclude other causes.
reference.pathophysiology: SIDS is thought to arise when an underlying vulnerability, an environmental stressor, and a critical developmental window coincide (the triple-risk model). The vulnerability is believed to involve abnormalities in brainstem regions that regulate arousal, cardiorespiratory control, and responses to hypoxia and hypercarbia, including serotonergic network dysfunction. When such an infant encounters a stressor, for example a prone position, rebreathing of expired air, or overheating during sleep, an impaired protective arousal and autonomic response may fail to correct hypoxia, leading to death.
additionalDifferentials: Accidental asphyxia or unsafe sleep-related suffocation
Inborn errors of metabolism (e.g. fatty acid oxidation defects)
Cardiac channelopathy or arrhythmia (e.g. long QT syndrome)
additionalInvestigations: Detailed death scene investigation and review of circumstances
Comprehensive clinical and family history review
Metabolic screening including postmortem samples where indicated
Genetic testing for cardiac channelopathies in selected cases
Microbiology and toxicology as part of the exclusion process
redFlags: Modifiable risk factors that mandate active safe-sleep counselling for prevention
Non-supine sleep position, soft bedding, or bed-sharing
Exposure to tobacco smoke before or after birth
History or scene findings suggesting suffocation or non-accidental injury
Recurrent unexplained infant deaths in a family, warranting careful evaluation
Prematurity or low birth weight increasing baseline risk
reference.prognosis: SIDS is by definition fatal; the clinical focus is prevention through consistent safe-sleep practices, which have substantially reduced incidence, and supportive bereavement care for affected families.
pitfalls: Assigning the label SIDS without a complete investigation that excludes other causes
Failing to deliver safe-sleep advice at every relevant contact
Overlooking an unsafe sleep environment as a contributing factor
Not considering metabolic or cardiac causes in apparently unexplained deaths
Neglecting sensitive support and follow-up for the bereaved family
management: Prioritise prevention through safe-sleep advice: supine sleeping on a firm flat surface, avoiding soft bedding and overheating
Promote room-sharing without bed-sharing, breastfeeding, pacifier use at sleep and routine immunisation
Counsel against maternal smoking, alcohol and drug use during pregnancy and around the infant
Provide compassionate bereavement support and referral to specialist support organisations for the family
Complete a thorough investigation — autopsy, death-scene review and, in selected cases, genetic testing for cardiac channelopathies — to exclude other causes and inform family counselling
Offer enhanced support and reinforced safe-sleep guidance for subsequent infants, such as a care-of-next-infant programme
